method: We kept every battery-electric model of model year 2025 or later in the EPA and DOE fueleconomy.gov data, listed each model once in its most efficient EPA-rated configuration of any model year in the data, and ranked on the EPA combined kWh per 100 miles. Because the EPA rates every wheel and trim configuration separately, the spread to the model's least efficient configuration is shown. Cost assumes 1,000 miles a month (our assumption) at the EIA U.S. average residential price, charged at home. Efficiency and range are EPA label figures, not our tests; real use varies with temperature, speed and load, and size and performance change the figure. We did not test any vehicle. The list mixes body styles and sizes, and a large SUV and a small sedan differ in efficiency mostly because of size, so compare within a class rather than across the whole list. A model that appears only as a model-year-2025 row, such as the Hyundai Ioniq 6 Standard Range, may no longer be sold new.
name: The most efficient electric cars, ranked by EPA kWh per 100 miles with the monthly cost to charge at home
scoring: each value scored against the best on the page (best = 1), times its weight; total out of 100

excluded.filter: one row per make + baseModel (newest model year, best configuration)
excluded.why: each model is shown a single time, in its most efficient EPA-rated configuration of any model year in the data, with the model year in its name; the gap to its least efficient configuration with the same drive type is shown beside it, so wheel and trim variants do not fill the list
